Pressure Switch Troubleshooting: How to Fix No Trip, Chattering, Setpoint Drift, Deadband and NO/NC Contact Faults in the Field

A pressure switch looks simple, yet one stuck contact can stop a pump or trip a whole compressor train. Below you will find field checks for every common fault, a fault table and a trip and reset calculator.

Not Tripping Chattering Setpoint Drift NO/NC Contacts Trip Calculator

Find out why a pressure switch does not trip, chatters or drifts away from its setpoint, using field checks in a fixed order. The fault table, the multimeter test and the calculator give every job a clear pass or fail.

Hello everyone, today we are going to learn pressure switch troubleshooting step by step, from a switch that never trips to a switch that chatters, drifts or has a failed NO or NC contact.
Quick Answer

How to do pressure switch troubleshooting step by step in the field?

Pressure switch troubleshooting means comparing the actual trip and reset pressures with the datasheet values and then checking contacts, wiring and the sensing element. Reset equals setpoint minus deadband for a rising trip. Example: a 10 bar high pressure switch with 1 bar deadband should trip near 10 bar and reset near 9 bar; if it trips at 11.2 bar, it has drifted and needs recalibration.

  1. Isolate the process and vent the impulse line safely.
  2. Check supply voltage, terminals and NO/NC wiring with a multimeter.
  3. Apply pressure slowly with a hand pump and reference gauge.
  4. Record the rising trip point and the falling reset point.
  5. Compare with setpoint, deadband and tolerance, then adjust or replace.

What Is Pressure Switch Troubleshooting?

Pressure switch troubleshooting means finding out why a switch does not change state at the correct pressure, or changes state when it should not. You combine a bench or in situ pressure test with electrical checks on the contacts, wiring and the receiving PLC or relay input.

Key Facts
  • Deadband, also called differential, is the gap between trip and reset pressure.
  • Tameson notes that mechanical switches typically have a deadband of 10 to 30 percent of the setpoint.
  • Most faults are wrong setpoint, pulsation, failed contacts, wiring or a damaged diaphragm.

If you are new to the device, first read how a pressure switch works. The rest of this pressure switch troubleshooting guide covers the faults you will meet in a plant.

Do You Know?

A pressure switch gives only two states, so it cannot show slow drift the way a transmitter can. Drift is usually found only during a trip test or after a real process upset.

Advertisement

Why Is My Pressure Switch Not Working?

A pressure switch usually stops working for one of five reasons: wrong setpoint, blocked or isolated impulse line, failed contacts, broken wiring or a damaged sensing element. The quickest way to separate them is to test the electrical side and the pressure side one at a time.

Start pressure switch troubleshooting with the simple checks: confirm the root valve is open and the line is clear, as in our impulse line testing procedure.

SymptomLikely CauseField CheckFix
Switch never tripsSetpoint too high, isolated tap, seized mechanismCompare local gauge with setpoint; apply test pressureOpen root valve, reset setpoint, replace if seized
ChatteringPulsation, narrow deadband, setpoint near normal pressureWatch gauge needle; log contact changesAdd snubber, widen deadband, move setpoint
Will not resetDeadband too wide or manual reset typeCheck nameplateAdjust deadband or press reset
Signal reversedWired to NO instead of NCCheck terminal C, NO, NC with meterRewire as per loop drawing
Intermittent signalLoose terminal or water in housingWiggle testRetighten, dry and seal
Quick Tip

Before you touch the setpoint screw, write down the as found trip and reset values. Without them you cannot prove whether the switch drifted or somebody changed it.

How to Test a Pressure Switch with a Multimeter

To test a pressure switch with a multimeter, isolate the power, connect the meter in continuity or resistance mode across common and NO, and slowly raise the pressure until the reading changes from open to closed. Then lower the pressure slowly to find the reset point where the contact opens again.

Fluke describes this same manual method for pressure switch troubleshooting and calibration. The difference between the rising set point and falling reset readings is the deadband.

1
Make it safe
Take a permit, isolate power and process, and vent trapped pressure.
2
Identify terminals
Find C, NO and NC; the OMEGA PSW300 guide marks them this way.
3
Check at rest
C to NO reads open and C to NC reads near zero ohms.
4
Ramp up slowly
Use a hand pump and reference gauge in small steps.
5
Record trip
Note the value when the meter changes state, three times.
6
Ramp down
Lower pressure slowly and note the reset value.

The reference gauge should be at least four times more accurate than the switch tolerance. Our guide on test uncertainty ratio explains this 4 to 1 target.

Once the fault is fixed, follow pressure switch calibration in 8 simple steps to record the as left values.

Field Tip
Never ramp quickly through the setpoint. The gauge lags the diaphragm and you record a false trip that looks like drift.

Pressure Switch Troubleshooting Calculator for Trip and Reset Point

This calculator works out the expected reset point from the setpoint and deadband, then checks your measured trip and reset values against the allowed tolerance. Pressure switch troubleshooting then ends in a plain pass or fail.

Rising trip: Reset = Setpoint minus Deadband
Falling trip: Reset = Setpoint + Deadband
Allowed error = Range × Tolerance % ÷ 100
Trip error = Measured trip minus Setpoint
Reset error = Measured reset minus Expected reset
Trip and Reset Point Tolerance Check
Result
Expected reset 9.00 bar, trip error 0.30 bar, reset error 0.10 bar, allowed 0.32 bar, measured deadband 1.20 bar: PASS

Solved example: a 0 to 16 bar high pressure switch is set at 10 bar with 1 bar deadband and 2 percent tolerance. The measured trip of 10.3 bar and reset of 9.1 bar are checked below.

Expected reset = 10 minus 1 = 9.00 bar
Allowed error = 16 × 2 ÷ 100 = 0.32 bar
Trip error = 10.3 minus 10 = 0.30 bar
Reset error = 9.1 minus 9 = 0.10 bar
Measured deadband = 1.20 bar, result PASS

If your gauge reads in psi, convert first with the online pressure unit converter or our psi to bar tool. For error in percent of span, use the calibration error calculator.

Why Does a Pressure Switch Chatter?

A pressure switch chatters when the process pressure moves back and forth across the setpoint faster than the deadband can absorb. Pulsation from pumps and compressors, a deadband that is too narrow, and a setpoint placed too close to normal operating pressure are the three main causes.

Whitman Controls notes that contacts bouncing near the set point confuse PLC logic and shorten relay life. It recommends a wider deadband and a snubber to smooth rapid pulses.

PulsationPump causes fast pressure swings.
CrossingPressure crosses the setpoint.
No marginNarrow deadband resets at once.
CureSnubber, wider deadband or delay.

See pressure snubber selection for snubber types, and deadband in pressure switches for why a wider gap cures hunting.

Do You Know?

Tameson explains that piston switches offer wide deadbands, while diaphragm and bourdon tube switches offer limited ones. A diaphragm switch on a pulsating discharge may chatter even when calibrated.

A short on delay timer in the PLC can mask bounce, much as switch debouncing does. On a safety trip, never hide chatter this way without a review.

How Do I Know If My Pressure Switch Is Bad?

A pressure switch is bad when it still fails to trip or reset within tolerance after the setpoint is corrected, or its contacts show high resistance. Visible signs include fluid inside the housing, corroded terminals and a setpoint screw that changes nothing.

Contact failure

Pitted or welded contacts read high resistance or stay closed.

Best for: Resistance check C to NO and C to NC
Electrical
Diaphragm damage

A ruptured diaphragm stops response or leaks fluid.

Best for: Overpressure or aggressive media
Mechanical
Setpoint drift

Trip value moves after vibration or overpressure.

Best for: Comparing with last calibration
Calibration
Wiring fault

Loose cores or wrong terminals reverse the signal.

Best for: Loop check to PLC input
Wiring

A closed contact should read near zero ohms, so several ohms or a jumping value means wear. Prove the cable with insulation resistance testing after disconnecting the PLC card.

Myth: If the switch clicks, it is working.
Fact: The contact can be pitted and open even when it clicks; measure resistance.
Myth: The setpoint screw fixes every wrong trip.
Fact: A damaged diaphragm or spring needs replacement, not adjustment.
Myth: Chattering always means a faulty switch.
Fact: Most chatter comes from pulsation or a narrow deadband.
Quick Tip

Keep a spare switch with the same range and contact type in store. Swapping and bench testing is often faster than fault finding in a hazardous area.

NO and NC Contact and Wiring Faults

Wiring faults show up as a reversed, frozen or flickering signal. Most come from using NO where the loop drawing asks for NC, or from loose terminals.

Safety trips are wired fail safe, so the contact is closed when healthy and opens on a trip or broken wire. Check against pressure switch wiring with NO and NC before changing terminals.

Healthy Wiring Signs
  • PLC input LED matches the contact state
  • Glands tight and housing dry
  • Ferrules fitted and screws tight
Faulty Wiring Signs
  • Signal reversed against alarm logic
  • Input flickers when cable moves
  • Green oxide or water in terminals

Match the wiring with the card type using sinking and sourcing in PLC. After rewiring, do an instrument loop check up to the HMI alarm.

Setpoint Drift and Wrong Deadband

Setpoint drift is the slow movement of the trip value away from the set value, while a wrong deadband means the reset point is too close to or too far from the trip. Both are found only by a rising and falling pressure test.

Drift comes from spikes above the proof pressure rating, vibration and temperature swings. OMEGA advises setpoints between 20 and 100 percent of range and warns that running at proof pressure may shift the setpoint.

In the OMEGA PSW300, adjuster B sets the rising operating point and adjuster A sets the falling reset. See setpoint and deadband configuration, and always recheck the trip after setting the reset.

Pressure Switch Troubleshooting Checklist for the Field

Work through this checklist in order during pressure switch troubleshooting so nothing is missed. It runs from isolation to the process side, then the electrical checks and finally the records.

  • Permit taken, process isolated and impulse line vented
  • Root valve and impulse line clear
  • Contact state at rest checked on C, NO and NC
  • Trip and reset recorded three times
  • Deadband within nameplate limits
  • Snubber fitted on pulsating service
  • As found and as left values recorded

Record values as shown in as found and as left records. With good records you can spot a drifting switch before it causes a shutdown.

When Should You Replace a Pressure Switch with a Transmitter?

Replace a mechanical switch with a transmitter or an electronic switch when the same unit keeps drifting, chattering or failing despite correct installation. With a continuous signal you can see the trend before the trip happens.

Compare options in pressure switch vs pressure transmitter and IO Link electronic switches. Under IEC 61511, nuisance trips also raise the spurious trip rate.

Pressure Switch Troubleshooting FAQ

What is the first step in pressure switch troubleshooting on a running plant?

The first step is to compare the local gauge reading with the switch setpoint and confirm the impulse line is open. Many no trip complaints end here because the root valve was closed or the tap was plugged.

Only after that should you isolate the switch and test its contacts.

What is the difference between setpoint, reset point and deadband in a pressure switch?

The setpoint is the pressure where the contact changes state, and the reset point is where it changes back. Deadband is the difference between them, so a 10 bar setpoint with a 9 bar reset gives a 1 bar deadband.

A wider deadband reduces chatter, while a narrow one suits alarms.

How to calculate the reset point of a pressure switch step by step?

For a rising trip, subtract the deadband from the setpoint, so 10 bar minus 1 bar gives a 9 bar reset. For a falling low pressure trip, add the deadband instead, so 2 bar plus 0.5 bar gives 2.5 bar.

Why does my pressure switch chatter near the setpoint on a pump discharge?

It chatters because pump pulsation moves pressure across the setpoint faster than the deadband can absorb. A snubber, a wider deadband or moving the setpoint further away from normal pressure usually stops it.

Confirm the cure by logging contact changes for one shift.

How do you check NO and NC contacts of a pressure switch with a multimeter?

Set the meter to resistance and measure C to NO and C to NC at zero pressure. NO should read open and NC near zero ohms, and both must swap state when the switch trips.

This simple check is the core of electrical pressure switch troubleshooting.

What are common mistakes during pressure switch testing in the field?

The most common mistake is ramping pressure too fast, which records a false trip value. Others include skipping as found readings, using a gauge less accurate than the switch and forgetting to retest.

Always finish pressure switch troubleshooting with a final as left test.

Which pressure switch is best for pulsating or high vibration service?

A piston type or electronic switch with adjustable deadband and delay is usually best for pulsating service. Fit a snubber and mount the switch on a bracket or panel away from the vibrating pipe.

This prevents fatigue of the diaphragm and early setpoint drift.

What We Learn Today

  • Pressure switch troubleshooting starts at the process tap and gauge, then moves to contacts, wiring and the sensing element in a fixed order.
  • Reset point equals setpoint minus deadband for a rising trip, and the measured values must stay within the allowed tolerance of the range.
  • Chattering is usually caused by pulsation or narrow deadband, and is cured with a snubber, wider deadband or a better placed setpoint.
